topic.subject: social
topic.title: Globe: latitudes and longitudes
topic.scope: Equator, heat zones, Prime Meridian, longitude and time, Indian Standard Time

misconceptions.statement: The Equator is a physical line drawn on the Earth's surface.
misconceptions.why: Students often confuse the lines on a map or globe with actual markings on the ground.
misconceptions.fix: The Equator is an imaginary line used by geographers to divide the Earth into Northern and Southern Hemispheres.

probe.question: If you travel to the Equator, what color will the line be painted on the ground?
probe.wrong_answer: It will be a white or yellow line like a road marking.

misconceptions.statement: The Earth is perfectly flat like a map.
misconceptions.why: Students spend most of their time looking at flat paper maps in textbooks.
misconceptions.fix: The Earth is a sphere, and a globe is a better model because it shows the true shape of the Earth.

probe.question: Why do we use a globe instead of just a map?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the globe is just a toy, but maps are the real shape of the world.

misconceptions.statement: The Torrid Zone is hot because it is closer to the Sun.
misconceptions.why: Students often assume that 'hotter' must mean 'physically closer' to the heat source.
misconceptions.fix: The Torrid Zone is hot because it receives direct rays from the Sun due to its position relative to the Equator, not because it is closer in distance.

probe.question: Why is the Torrid Zone hotter than the Frigid Zone?
probe.wrong_answer: Because the Torrid Zone is physically nearer to the Sun in space.

misconceptions.statement: Time is the same everywhere on Earth at the same moment.
misconceptions.why: Students generalize their local experience of time to the entire planet.
misconceptions.fix: Because the Earth rotates from west to east, different longitudes experience sunrise and sunset at different times.

probe.question: If it is noon in London, is it also noon in Tokyo?
probe.wrong_answer: Yes, noon is the same time for everyone on Earth.

misconceptions.statement: The Prime Meridian is the line where the day officially begins.
misconceptions.why: Students confuse the Prime Meridian (0 degrees longitude) with the International Date Line.
misconceptions.fix: The Prime Meridian is the reference line for time zones, but the International Date Line is where the calendar date changes.

probe.question: Where do we change the date when crossing the globe?
probe.wrong_answer: At the Prime Meridian in Greenwich.
